_meta.purpose: Named scenario stories for the judge surface. Each one is a real MissionInput run through the real engine at request time, never a stored result. The set exists so a judge can see the range of the engine in about a minute without typing anything, and so no screen can ever show an empty state.
_meta.rule: Every scenario must end somewhere DIFFERENT. A set of buttons that all produce the same verdict reads as one hardcoded answer and costs the credibility of the one that matters. engine/__tests__/scenarios.test.ts asserts the outcomes actually differ.
_meta.provenance: Orbits and ballistic coefficients are drawn from the same NRLMSISE-00 decay table the verdict uses (data/decay-table.json). Dates are illustrative and are labelled as such: these are worked examples of the regulatory clocks, not records of real missions. The one real seeded mission is GT-1 in data/missions/gt-1.json.

scenarios.name: Disposal is fine, the schedule is not
scenarios.demonstrates: The two axes come apart. At 400 km the satellite reenters well inside the FCC five-year limit, so disposal is clear, and the licensing campaign is still late enough that regulatory deadlines are violated. Passing one test is not passing the other.

scenarios.name: Same orbit, opposite legal answer
scenarios.demonstrates: The differentiator. At 550 km the same satellite is compliant near solar maximum and non-compliant near solar minimum, so the launch window decides the legal outcome rather than the design.

scenarios.name: A camera puts NOAA in front of the FCC
scenarios.demonstrates: Imaging Earth makes the NOAA CRSRA licence a hard predecessor of FCC grant, adding a 60-day statutory clock that most planning tools never surface.

scenarios.name: No launch vehicle yet
scenarios.demonstrates: Without a launch-vehicle determination the 47 CFR 97.207(g) dual clock cannot start, so the pre-space notification window is undefined and the campaign has no anchor.

scenarios.name: Above 600 km, the propulsion decision
scenarios.demonstrates: At 700 km atmospheric drag alone will not bring the satellite down inside five years, so the mission needs propulsion or a drag device before the FCC will grant.

scenarios.name: Delivery is in ten weeks
scenarios.demonstrates: The launch provider's delivery date is a hard wall. With the campaign started late, multiple regulatory nodes are already past their latest start and the mission is heading for demanifest.
